stem: developed to even include the missed cases. Which one is high?
OptD: Negative predictive value Oxford Handbook of Clinical Medicine ● A sensitive test is chosen when the priority is detecting all possible cases. When a question says “include missed cases” or “avoid missing disease” = High Sensitivity (well-established across major medical textbooks and guidelines). High sensitivity tests minimize false negatives and are used when the goal is not to miss cases (screening tests). If the stem says: ● screening ● detect early ● avoid missing cases ● include missed cases Always think HIGH SENSITIVITY. “Developed to even include the missed cases” means: The test aims to detect as many true disease cases as possible, including cases that might otherwise be missed. This describes high sensitivity.

67 year old man 6hours post femoral artery surgery developed swelling and worsening neurological signs (Stem exactly like this)
OptD: nerve repair fasciotomy ?? I suspect acute compartment syndrome due to reperfusion injury after vascular surgery. After revascularization: ● Capillary leak = increase compartment pressure. ● Muscle & nerve ischemia = neurologic deficits. ● Can cause permanent damage within 6–8 hours. Fasciotomy is a surgical procedure where the doctor cuts open the fascia (the tough connective tissue surrounding muscles) to relieve dangerous pressure inside a muscle compartment. Muscles in the arms and legs are enclosed in tight spaces called compartments. When swelling or bleeding occurs (after trauma, surgery, or reperfusion): ➡ Pressure increases. ➡ Blood flow decreases. ➡ Nerves and muscles become ischemic. ➡ Permanent damage can occur within hours. A fasciotomy releases the pressure and saves the limb.

Hairdresser came to the emergency department with a swollen bulb of the thumb finger after getting a stick from the tools she’s using, Nail bed is intact?
OptD: Cellulitis ● A deep infection of the distal pulp (fingertip pad). ● Causes tense, swollen, very painful bulb of the finger. ● Usually follows a penetrating injury (like a stick from tools — common in hairdressers, barbers, etc.). ● Nail bed is intact (important clue). ● Paronychia = Infection around the nail fold ● Onychomycosis = Fungal infection of the nail. ● Cellulitis = Diffuse skin infection, not localized tense pulp swelling. Felon is dangerous because the fingertip pulp is divided into multiple septal compartments, so pressure builds up = risk of ischemia and osteomyelitis.

A 7-year-old boy has had recurrent upper and lower respiratory tract bacterial infections since infancy. On examination, he has eczema and areas of ecchymosis on his skin. His brother and a paternal uncle are similarly affected (see lab results). Hb 108 112-165 g/L WBC t.6 4.5-10.5 x 109/L Platelets count 40 150-400 × 109/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
OptD: DiGeorge syndrome Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WAS) is a rare X-linked recessive genetic immunodeficiency affecting mostly males, characterized by the triad of low platelet count (microthrombocytopenia), severe eczema, and recurrent infections. It is caused by mutations in the WASgene, which impairs immune cell function and disrupts platelet production. Management includes antibiotics, immunoglobulin infusions, and definitive treatment through stem cell transplantation.
